lesson.title: Best, Average, and Worst Case: Same Algorithm, Different Inputs
lesson.summary: Best, average, and worst case describe how a single algorithm's running time can differ depending on the specific input it receives, not different algorithms or different Big-O growth rates.
lesson.body:
So far, this unit has mostly discussed time complexity as if each algorithm has one single growth rate. In reality, many algorithms perform differently depending on what data they are given, even for inputs of the exact same size n. Best case, average case, and worst case are three ways of describing that variation for one algorithm, not three different algorithms.

Linear search makes this concrete.

def linear_search(values, target):
    for i, v in enumerate(values):
        if v == target:
            return i
    return -1

If target happens to be the first element, linear_search returns almost immediately, that is the best case, O(1) for that particular call, even though the function is generally described as O(n). If target is the last element, or is not in the list at all, the loop has to check all n elements, that is the worst case, O(n). If target is equally likely to be anywhere in the list, the average case involves checking roughly n/2 elements on average, which is still O(n) once you drop the constant factor of one half, but it represents a genuinely different scenario than the worst case.

This is the same function throughout, linear_search does not change; only the input, where target happens to sit, or whether it exists at all, changes. That is the core idea this concept builds on from Time Complexity: time complexity describes growth rate for a given scenario, and best, average, and worst case tell you which scenario you are measuring.

By default, when a Big-O bound is given without qualification, it almost always refers to the worst case. This is a deliberate, useful convention: the worst case is a guarantee. If an algorithm is O(n) in the worst case, you know it will never do more than roughly n units of work, no matter what input a user, an adversary, or bad luck throws at it. Average case can be more informative about typical real world performance, but it depends on assumptions about the distribution of inputs, like target being equally likely to be anywhere, that may or may not hold for your actual data, which is why worst case remains the default and most trustworthy bound.

Some algorithms have identical best, average, and worst case behavior. sum_all from the Linear Time chapter always adds up every element no matter what the values are, so its best, average, and worst case are all O(n). Other algorithms, like linear_search, or quicksort, whose worst case is O(n^2) but whose average case is O(n log n), can have dramatically different behavior across these scenarios, which is exactly why it matters to specify which case you are talking about whenever the answer is not obvious.
